chapter_theme: First songs at Tiruchengodu (திருச்செங்கோடு, 1 of 2), also called Nagagiri: the poet confesses his infatuation with courtesans and their arts, his begging songs to hard-hearted patrons, and a life of births bound by malam, and asks for the feet, for union with the devotees and for the wisdom of Agastya; the praise names Murugan the teacher of Siva and gives the Ramayana in brief.
structure_note: Short courtesan songs in the same metre (585 to 587), longer courtesan songs (590 to 594, 597), birth and malam (593, 595, 596), begging from patrons (589), union with devotees (588), and two short songs on Nagagiri (598, 599), the last in long syllables only.

585.reading: The poet asks whether, instead of coming with love to bow at Murugan's feet, he will keep thinking of women whose eyes are poison-filled lotuses and whose hair is full of bees, and wander deluded and fighting without end. The praise names Murugan son of the dancer of the hall, wearer of kadamba, whose vel ends the births of those who come and bow, and asks him to come with his red cock wherever the poet goes calling 'Kanda', at Tiruchengodu of red paddy and lotus.
585.nuance: சென்றே இடங்கள் கந்தா எனும்பொ(து) ... வரவேணும்: a plea for the god's company in daily wandering, not only at death. ஐம்பூதம் ஒன்ற நினையாமல் is unclear: perhaps 'not thinking of the five elements becoming one'.

586.reading: The poet asks that he not wither away, his life bursting with crowded desire, over women whose palms ache from playing ball, whose garlanded hair and lotus faces draw singing bees and whose breasts do harm, but that Murugan give his grace. The praise names Kanda, son of Hara and nephew of Mukunda, the one who split the hill, bridegroom of the celestial maiden, wearing a kadamba garland on his strong shoulders, at Tiruchengodu.
586.nuance: The song is short and conventional; the women are pictured at play (பந்தாடி அங்கை நொந்தார்), an image from love poetry. கன்றா விலங்கல் ஒன்றாறு கண்ட and the eight elephants sleeping at Tiruchengodu are hard to divide.

587.reading: The poet asks for grace so that he does not decline, forgetting Murugan's flower-decked feet, among women whose spear-like eyes defeat Kama's arrows and bewilder all who see them. The praise names Murugan nephew of Vishnu of the discus and conch, Kumaresa who stands as part of the devotees who melt in song and true friendship, joy of Siva who dances in the hall, at Tiruchengodu of red paddy.
587.nuance: நண்போதும் அன்பர் பங்காகி நின்ற குமரேசா: Murugan stands as a share of his devotees, close to them rather than above them.

588.reading: The poet, whose mind is confused and deluded in the way of union with women with carp eyes and sweet words, asks when he will be one with the devotees who think to lay their speech, knowledge, life and feeling on Murugan's lotus feet as a garland. The praise shows the hill split, the gods resettled and Indra's city flourishing, the demon armies of elephants, chariots, horses and foot ruined and the sea crying out, at Tiruchengodu of rich fields.
588.nuance: உரையையும் அறிவையும் உயிரையும் உணர்வையும் ... உரவாடு புனைதர: the whole self, speech, mind, life and feeling, is offered as a garland at the feet, and the goal is the company of devotees (அடியரொடு ஒன்றாக).

589.reading: The poet confesses going from place to place, begging and accepting, sinking in the fire of hunger, singing paltry poems shaped to the rules of Tamil grammar to iron-hearted men who show no pity, faltering, trembling and cringing in praise, and asks whether such a one can gain love for Murugan. The praise, in heavy wordplay, names Murugan who gave his arms to the hunter girl, the vel at Tiruchengodu, who grants joy to those who reach, feel, melt, bow and know him.
589.nuance: இயல் தண் தமிழ் நூலின் உடம்பாட்டுடன் பாட்டு இயம்பா: the poet's skill in correct Tamil is spent on patrons who do not pity. The rhyme runs in clusters (இறுங்கார்க் கிரும்பார்க் குநெஞ்சார்க் கிரங்கார்க்கு), which makes the splitting of the words partly uncertain.

590.reading: The poet asks not to perish in the sidelong glances of sinful women who melt thought and sight with words sweet as strained cane juice; he says he longs to receive the teaching that turns him away, and asks Murugan to say 'do not fear' so that he gives up the evil his mind plans by its deeds. The praise names the vel that cuts down the demon armies and the teacher through whom liberation bears fruit at once for those few who know how to call on his feet, at the towered Tiruchengodu.
590.nuance: விலக்கும் போதகம்: the teaching asked for is one that turns him back from women. அஞ்சேல் என: the plea is for the assuring word of the Lord, a common gesture (the hand of fearlessness) put into speech.

591.reading: The poet asks not to wander in the lewd, sorrowful trade of women who show rolling eyes and their breasts to many, deceive, and give the cane-sweet juice of their lips, and asks whether Murugan, whom Brahma, Vishnu and Siva the slayer of Death could not see, will protect him, let him hear the sweet words of the meaning, and look on him with grace. The praise names Murugan who drove out Sura hiding in deceit, who stands in the company of devotees in the kura groves, who wooed the hunter girl in the millet field, at Tiruchengodu in the Kongu country.
591.nuance: தொழில் பண்டாட்டம்: the courtesan's life is called a trade, a bargaining. பொருள் கொண்டாட்டத்து இன்ப வாக்யம்: perhaps the teaching sentence (vakya) of the true meaning, asked as a gift to the ear; the phrase is not certain.

592.reading: After a long head-to-foot portrait of courtesans who sell themselves, the poet says that, leaping into union with them, he has caught diseases and sunk in birth, and asks for the knowledge by which his deeds flee, so that coming the great way of bowing to the kadamba-garlanded feet his burning ends, he drinks the sea of nectar, approaches the coral-red form and chants 'radiant Muruga' with love. The praise names the goddess in many forms, Murugan the teacher and destroyer of Sura, Vishnu's deeds against Hiranya, Vali, Kumbhakarna and Ravana and his sport with the cowherd girls, Valli's beauty, and Tiruchengodu.
592.nuance: கோல விலை மாதர் and கலியநோய்கள் கொண்டே: the courtesans are named by their price and the poet names disease caught from them, a rare literal consequence in these songs. அமுத வாரி here is the nectar of grace, not Tirumular's yogic fluid.

593.reading: The poet says he never once thought to cut the rope of false birth, and, wounded, doubting and troubled, became a vessel of desire for cruel lotus-eyed women; he asks for good nature and the anklet-bearing red lotus feet, so that he may serve and prostrate at Tiruchengodu. The praise tells of Siva flaying the elephant to delight Uma, and of Murugan who explained the sense of the word 'thou' (தொம்பதம்) to Sambhu, the beautiful lord on the red peak.
593.nuance: சம்புவுக்குத் தொம்பதத்துப் பண்பு உரைத்து: தொம்பதம் is the 'tvam' of the Vedantic sentence tat tvam asi, so the familiar story of Murugan teaching Siva is here told in Vedantic terms rather than as the meaning of Om. The opening lines (பொங்கி முக்கிச் சங்கை பற்றிச் சிங்கி ஒத்த) are uncertain in sense.

594.reading: In a refrain of 'they show' (காட்டுவர்), the poet lists the courtesans' displays, the slow sidelong look, the back of the scented hair, turmeric-gold skin, false pity, agreement of heart, firm attachment, breasts, navel, conch-like neck, quarrels and pretended modesty, and asks whether he will stop showing longing for them. The praise names Murugan the guru whom his father worships, who drove off the enemies of a devotee who had adorned him with a golden pendant, who embraced the hunter girl, at Tiruchengodu in Kongu.
594.nuance: The refrain makes the whole courtship a show (காட்டுவர்), so that the poet's own feeling (இரங்கம் காட்டுவது) is the last display in the list. The devotee with the golden pendant (பைம்பொன் பதக்கம் பூட்டிய அன்பன்) is an allusion I cannot identify.

595.reading: In packed, clipped syllables the poet seems to say that, leaving true support for false, he cannot climb out of the sea of births of constant sorrow, maddened for honey-sweet women, while those who cherished Murugan's golden anklets came later and gained the good portion. The praise names Murugan of Tiruchengodu, lord of the millet-hill girl Valli, wearer of vetchi flowers, the pure one, the pearl, the lord of liberation.
595.nuance: மெய்ச்சார்வு அற்றே பொய்ச்சார்வு உற்றே: losing the support of truth for the support of the false is the clearest phrase. The song is a feat of doubled consonants (செச்சா லிச்சா லத்தே றிச்சே) and most of it can be divided several ways.

596.reading: The poet asks not to bind himself to women whose nature seeks to cause pain and to men who die harming others, and that, with birth full of sin and the evil of malam ended, Murugan give his two feet, rule him and tell him the sharp strength of grace so he reaches the high heaven. The praise shows the vel slaying the demons with bodies bathed in blood, the ghost hosts beating time with drums, and Murugan rejoicing on the peacock at Tiruchengodu of pools and lilies.
596.nuance: சுவர்க்கம் சேர: heaven is named as the goal, less common than release in these songs. The first lines (மலக்கங் கூடியே இன உயிர்க்கும் சேதமாகிய மரிக்கும் பேர்கள்) are uncertain.

597.reading: The poet lists courtesans who are venomous as cobras, whose eyes cut like swords, who call to anyone at all, dance along the streets, rouse hopes, loosen hair and sari and glitter with scent, and drown men in maya, and asks whether, caught in lust, he must wander in births of malam without the life of serving Murugan. The praise tells the Ramayana in order, Dasaratha's son guarding the sage's sacrifice, the stone made woman by his foot, the bow broken at Mithila, the exile, Vali and Ravana slain, and names Murugan the teacher of knowledge on the great Naga hill.
597.nuance: மலச் சனனம்: births are named as the work of malam. The Ramayana sequence in the praise is unusually complete. நெருவைப்பதி is a place name I cannot identify.

598.reading: A short song: the poet asks not to draw near Death and not to be born again on earth, and to be given the honey-nectar of the wisdom of the virtuous Agastya. The praise names Murugan hard for Vishnu and Brahma to reach, never parted from the great ascetics, the meaning of the four Vedas, the lord of Nagagiri.
598.nuance: சீல அகத்திய ஞான: probably the knowledge of Agastya, whom Murugan taught (see 28); it could also be read as 'the knowledge within' (அகத்து இய). The song asks for knowledge as the escape from death and birth.

599.reading: A song made almost wholly of long syllables: through strings of vocatives the poet seems to ask the lord of the earth to protect his life in danger, lest he, a sinner, fall into the burning ground. The praise is a chain of names, Kama-like in beauty, the playful child, wearer of kadamba, the son, the Vel, the flower, the king, the god, lord of the gods.
599.nuance: யாபத்து எனது ஆவி ... காவாய் ... ஈமத்து உகலாமோ: 'protect my life in danger; should I fall into the pyre?' is the only clear plea. The song is a metrical feat (தாமா தாமா லாபா லோகா) in which nearly every word can be split another way.

links.note: Both confess the court poet's begging: 579 praised the man who never gives as Kubera, 589 sang correct Tamil verse to iron-hearted men who show no pity. Both make this, not only desire, a reason he did not seek the Lord.

The Kural says nothing degrades the tongue more than begging, even water for a cow; 589 shows that degradation in the poet himself, trembling and cringing as he sings for gifts, and asks whether such a tongue can gain love for the Lord.

The song asks to be one with the devotees who lay their speech, knowledge, life and feeling as a garland on the lotus feet (உரையையும் அறிவையும் உயிரையும் உணர்வையும் உன்பாத கஞ்ச மலர்மீதே ... புனைதர). Tirumular describes Nandi taking the disciple's body, wealth and life with poured water and setting his feet on him (உடல்பொருள் ஆவி உதகத்தாற் கொண்டு ... நொடியின் அடிவைத்து). The same total giving of the self appears in the Tirumanthiram as a guru's rite of taking and in the song as the devotee's own garland at the feet.

In 589 the poet confesses he sang paltry poems, correct by the rules of Tamil grammar, to iron-hearted patrons who show no pity (இரங்கார்க் கியற்றண் டமிழ்நூலின் உடம்பாட் டுடன்பாட் டியம்பா ... புன்கவிபாடி), driven by hunger. In 613 the same trade is seen from outside: poets who praise men as the dark cloud riding Garuda, slip in their names and steal from old sayings (அவர்பெயர் செருகி ... திருடி ஒருபடி நெருடி). The later song turns the earlier personal confession into a portrait of the patron-poet's craft.

The song asks for the teaching that turns him back (விலக்கும் போதகம்) and for the Lord to say 'do not fear' so that he gives up the evil his mind plans (விடற்கு அஞ்சேல் என அருள்வாயே). Tirumular says the goddess who gives the means rooted out danger from his heart, held craving down and said 'fear not' (அவாவை அடக்கிவைத்து அஞ்சல் என்றாளே). The song asks for exactly what the Tirumanthiram verse reports as done: the word of reassurance coming together with the curbing of desire.

The song names the courtesan who shows her breasts to many (கொங்கை நோக்கப் பலர்க்குங் காட்டி) and calls her life a trade (தொழில் பண்டாட்டம்). The Kural says those of refined understanding will not plunge into the base charms of those whose goodness belongs to everyone (பொதுநலத்தார் புன்னலம் தோயார்). The Kural's பொதுநலம், beauty held in common, is what the song shows in action, and the song asks Murugan for the knowledge the Kural assumes the wise already have.

Both songs name disease caught from courtesans as the literal consequence of the pleasure: 592 says that leaping into union with women named by their price (கோல விலை மாதர்) he has taken diseases (கலிய நோய்கள் கொண்டே), and 461 shows the man who paid wandering with swelling sores and festering eyes until onlookers cover their eyes (கண்டவர்க்குக் கண் புதைப்ப). Read together they show the disease motif is a recurring warning in the courtesan songs, in 592 tied to birth and in 461 to public shame.

The praise says Murugan explained to Sambhu the nature of the tvam-pada (சம்புவுக்குத் தொம்பதத்துப் பண்பு உரைத்து). Tirumular names the three padas of the Vedantic sentence, tat-pada, tvam-pada and asi-pada (தற்பதம் தொம்பதம் தானாம் அசிபதம்), as the soul, the Supreme and Siva within turiya. The pairing shows that the Vedantic 'thou' already had a Saiva reading in Tamil, and that the song makes it the content of Murugan's lesson to Siva in place of the usual meaning of Om.

In its refrain the song lists what the courtesans show, among them false pity and agreement of heart (வஞ்சத் திரக்கங் காட்டுவர் நெஞ்சிற் பொருத்தங் காட்டுவர்). The Kural says the weak-hearted touch the shoulders of women who join with them while tending other things in their hearts (பிறநெஞ்சிற் பேணிப் புணர்பவர்). Both locate the deceit in a heart that is shown as one thing and holds another; the song's காட்டுவர் makes the Kural's divided heart into a performance.

The song's clearest phrase is that, leaving the support of truth for the support of the false (மெய்ச்சார்வு அற்றே பொய்ச்சார்வு உற்றே), he cannot leave the sea of births. The Kural says a wretched birth comes from the confusion that takes what is not real for real (பொருளல்லவற்றைப் பொருளென்று உணரும் மருளான் ஆம் மாணாப் பிறப்பு). Both make the mistaking of false for true the cause of birth, the song as a confession and the Kural as a general law.

The song asks that the birth full of the evil of malam end and that he reach high heaven (மலத்தின் தீமை கூடிய பிறப்புந் தீர ... உயர் சுவர்க்கஞ் சேர). Tirumular says those freed of the five malams become Siva, while those still in the malams' darkness are the kind that go from earth to heaven and hell (பாரின்கண் விண்நரகம் புகும் பான்மையர்). On the reading that the song names heaven as the goal after malam ends, the two conflict: for Tirumular heaven belongs to the round of the bound, not to its end; both verses are uncertain in places.

The song pictures courtesans who call to anyone at all and dance along the street (யாவராயினும் நத்தி அழைப்பவர் தெருவூடே). The Naladiyar says such women, whatever believable words they speak, belong to no one but their own bodies (யார்க்கும் தமரல்லர் தம்உடம்பினார்). The two halves fit: those who call everyone are kin to no one, and the song adds that this drowns the man in maya and births of malam.

In 28 the poet asks that Death not call him and praises Murugan as the one who spoke sweet Tamil to delight the sage of Pothiyai (பொதியவரை முநிவனக மகிழ ... இனியதமிழ் பகர்வோனே). In 598 he asks not to draw near Death nor be born on earth, and to be given the honey-nectar of the knowledge of virtuous Agastya (சீலஅகத்திய ஞான தேனமுதைத் தருவாயே). The later song asks for himself what the earlier one says Murugan gave the sage, and makes that knowledge the remedy against Death and birth.

source_issues: Song 590: one corrupt character in வயலு஡ரா (line 14), probably வயலூரா; also பாவிகளள் (line 3) with a doubled letter.
Song 594: one corrupt character in வயலு஡ரா (line 12).
Songs 597 to 599 name the shrine நாகமலை / நாககிரி, another name for Tiruchengodu, not the heading's name.
